connection_type: I'm an interested observer — no direct personal connection
disclosure_text:
I have no personal experience on this topic, but I grew up in an area where classmates belonged to various religious groups that had restrictions they had to abide by. At school growing up we always said the Lords Prayer after singing the national anthem and I remember one family moved to the area and the children had to stand outside the classroom for this part of the day. I remember feeling badly for the girl in my class that had to do this. Eventually, the school stopped doing the prayer and the girl no longer had to stand outside the door in the morning.
There was also another religious group in my area where all the women had to wear dresses and have their hair a certain way. The children could not watch television or listen to the music all the other children listened to. I saw how they were often left out from group discussions and how that affected them.
Throughout my life working and travelling, I have seen how people are treated differently than others for no other reason than the color of their skin or their religious views.
micronarrative: Having grown up in a small community, I have seen first hand how people can take a post that should be seen as positive and twist it around to fit some other narrative. When the person doing so is well known in the community with a lot of followers, it does not take long before others have joined in their cause. It makes me sad to think that people are so quick to think badly of others when they are not fully informed and when they think there is a threat to their "culture". Most of the people in my community go to church on Sundays but that is where their religious ties would end. People that would go to church on Sunday and act like they follow the word of God can sometimes be the worst individuals in their daily lives. I enjoyed going to Sunday school and reading and doing crafts with the other children. It did give a greater sense that the community was there for you when you were at church on Sunday. People would certainly speak with more kindness on those days. I was always fascinated by people being able to make their own clothing so I saw it as a positive. I actually enjoy sewing and crocheting so I make things for my son all the time. He likes that other kids don't have the same things.

You mentioned growing up in a small community—what was the dominant cultural or religious makeup of that place, and where did you fit within it?
Most of the people in my community go to church on Sundays but that is where their religious ties would end.
In that context, did the language used in those Sunday services differ from how people spoke in their daily lives or at work?

I would say that most people would be on their best behavior when it came to Sunday church service. They would dress nicely and act neighborly. I enjoyed going to Sunday school and reading and doing crafts with the other children. It did give a greater sense that the community was there for you when you were at church on Sunday. People would certainly speak with more kindness on those days.
Did that emphasis on appearance and "best behavior" feel like a financial burden for families in your community, or was it just a standard expectation?

I never really considered it before, but I am sure that it probably did feel like a financial burden for some of the families as they had multiple children and everyone had nice clothing. I know that my mom always made sure that I had dress clothes and shoes for church and I always had nice new tights or pantyhose to wear. I think that some people in the community made their own clothing since it was much cheaper to buy fabric, but they always looked nice.
How did you perceive the families who made their own clothes compared to those who bought theirs, and did that distinction affect how you viewed their standing in the community?

I was always fascinated by people being able to make their own clothing so I saw it as a positive. I was often jealous of the girls that had unique, pretty dresses that their moms had made for them. At the time, I did not really consider that they were doing it to save money. I actually enjoy sewing and crocheting so I make things for my son all the time. He likes that other kids don't have the same things.
Does your son ever face questions or comments from peers about wearing unique, handmade items, and how does he navigate those interactions?
